newsitem.title: JAPAN: JGBs end higher as investors flock to new bond.
newsitem.headline: JGBs end higher as investors flock to new bond.

text.p: Key March 10-year Japanese government bond (JGB) futures closed higher on Wednesday on dealers' short-covering following a better-than-expected showing for the newly auctioned 10-year JGBs.
"We had placed short positions to hedge. But our fears that the new bond may not be sold well turned out to be totally imaginary," said a dealer at a "Big-Four" brokerage house.
Some dealers said foreigners were also buying the March contract ahead of a shift in its benchmark status later this week. The March closed up 0.26 at 126.36 with 50,373 contracts changing hands.
The contract opened at a day's low of 126.20. Its session high was 126.53.
The dealer said the new bond was sold to regional and public investors in Japan as well as foreigners.
But a dealer at another Big-Four brokerage said: "We saw firm bids from regional investors for the new issue. But city banks and other major investors barely bought it."

Traders said accepted bids by three of Japan's Big Four brokerage houses accounted for 70 percent of Tuesday's 10-year JGB auction. Their sales to regional and agricultural financial institutions seem to have gone well, they said.
A dealer at a long-term credit bank's securities unit said: "Major investors showed hardly any interest in the new March issue as they preferred buying the February one."
The new bond re-opened the 2.6 percent 193rd bond and has the same maturity date. But it was overbought when compared with the February issue, traders said.
Meanwhile, fairly good demand was detected for municipal and government-guaranteed bonds launched today as they are unlisted and were priced under par, traders said.
The yield of cash benchmark 182nd 10-year JGBs stood at 2.380 percent at 0706 GMT, down 0.020 from Tuesday's finish.
Some dealers said a brief rise in the March contract above a resistance point of 126.40 was partly due to foreigners' buy-backs ahead of a shift in its benchmark status.

"Hedge funds which had placed large-lot short positions for the last three weeks or so seemed to be covering a part of these shorts ahead of a benchmark shift expected later this month," said a dealer at a city bank's securities unit.
When turnover of the June contract exceeds that of the March, the market considers June to be the new benchmark. The June ended up 0.25 at 124.96 in turnover of 17,380 contracts.
